field_updates.description: Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and scholarly research meet in varied academic practices. Oral histories, family relationships, archival inquiry and collaborations contribute different resources; authority and methods remain situated.
field_updates.date_label: Earlier examples 1615–1938; 1970s–90s growth · baseline through 2000; selected 2010 intervention

date_span.basis: c. 1615/1616 dates the earliest selected manuscript witness, not the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge or a common academic field. Selected nineteenth-century and interwar practices precede the 1970s–90s academic/methodological growth. The baseline selection is through 2000; a separately marked 2010 article supplies one selected later intervention.

field_updates.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier selected writing includes Guaman Poma (c. 1615/1616), Cusick (checked 1828 edition), Apess (1836), Te Rangikāheke (manuscripts before 1854), and Cree/Tainui interwar work. Twentieth-century examples include McNickle (1949), Deloria (1969), Adams and LaRocque (1975), Dickason (1984, 1992), Sioui (1989), Walker (1990), Kameʻeleihiwa (1992), O’Brien (1997), Wilson (1996), and Smith (1999). See the distinct approaches for works, collaborators and evidence limits. Related scholarship includes Miller, White, Harris and Lutz; Stó:lō field-school practice credits community and university participants. Leddy’s 2010 reflection supplies a separately dated later case.
field_updates.scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

edges.evidence_note: Stó:lō community and university participants combine different research resources in this particular field-school programme. This comparison records overlapping practice; it does not make either field the origin of the other.
Harris’s 1997 geographical inquiry offers a specific connection to histories of Indigenous–settler land relations. This comparison does not assert adoption of his methods by Indigenous historians.
